name: Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth
strategy: Concentrated long book in small/mid-cap cloud, AI-infra, and fintech compounders with secular demand, riding small-cap and software leadership while avoiding weak crypto.

positions.thesis: Promoted to largest position because it absorbs the NET exposure at less than half the multiple, and because a fact appeared this week that I did not have before. Palo Alto reportedly held acquisition talks with Datadog before spending $28bn elsewhere; a named strategic acquirer at the table is not a takeout thesis, but it is independent evidence about what an informed buyer thinks the asset is worth, and it puts a soft floor under a stock that is 19% below its $292.72 high. On the numbers it is the best risk/reward in the software half by a distance: $236.98 against 46 analysts at $285.18 for 20.3% headroom, 36% revenue growth, 89.5x forward versus NET's 203x, and genuinely profitable rather than promising to be. Crucially the de-rate already happened here — the 18% post-earnings drop on the OpenAI usage guidance is why the headroom exists, so I am buying after the multiple compression rather than before it, which is precisely the opposite of my position in NET. I take it to 18% and no further because 89.5x is still a rate-sensitive multiple in a hiking regime and the single-largest-customer concentration is an unresolved counterparty exposure that can gap again. Stop moved in from -20% to -18%, around $194: with the position two points larger the same percentage stop is a bigger dollar risk, and -18% still sits below the whole post-earnings gap zone so it protects against a trend break rather than firing on ordinary volatility. Take-profit cut from +30% to +25%, around $296, which sits just above both consensus and the 52-week high — I would rather anchor the exit to a price the market has actually paid than to a number I invented.

Added two points because all three revenue engines improved this week while the stock went down 3.8% from where I bought it, and that gap is the whole argument. Bitcoin ran from roughly $72k to $80,258 on Thursday, the first print above $80k since May, on $1.92bn of spot-ETF inflows in a week — the strongest since October 2025 — which lifts crypto transaction revenue. Prediction markets and the MIAXdx joint venture are pulling a fresh wave of street targets. And interest revenue is already up 278% year on year, so a September hike raises the roughly one-third of revenue that is net interest rather than lowering it. That last point is why this is the leg I add to rather than any of the software: it is the only holding in the book whose earnings power is helped by the exact policy shift that is hurting the other four, which makes it a real internal hedge in a long-only book. I have to be honest that Friday cuts against me — it fell 5.01%, worse than any holding, on the day the hike was priced in, which says the market currently trades it as high beta first and an NII beneficiary second, and bitcoin slipping back below $78k on the same headline is part of that. So I add two points, not five: the fundamental improvement is real and the price has not paid for it yet, but I am not going to insist the tape is wrong about correlation on the same afternoon it told me otherwise. The Clarity Act remains a bill that has been called for and not passed, with only a procedural Senate vote scheduled. Stop stays wide at -20%, near $83, because at beta 2.32 anything tighter is noise; take-profit at +45% lands near $151, just under the $153.86 52-week high.

Added a point on valuation, which in this specific week is a risk decision rather than a return one. At $14.30 it trades 14.76x forward against 44% revenue growth and a 33% ROE, comfortably the cheapest thing I own, and it is the only holding where the multiple has almost no room left to compress — in a book whose central risk is now multiple compression from a rising discount rate, that is worth paying for. Two genuinely new facts since last week: a $1.0bn buyback authorisation, which is a first for this company and puts a bid under the stock, and Mexican banking authorisations that turn the second market from a distribution experiment into a licensed bank. The Q2 base is a first-ever billion-dollar net income quarter, $2.47bn revenue up 52%, and 22 analysts sit at $18.78 for 31% upside. The honest risk is that higher US rates pressure emerging-market currencies and flows, and it fell 3.9% on Friday for exactly that reason — but that is a translation and sentiment effect on a business whose earnings are driven by Brazilian and Mexican credit card and deposit penetration, not by the US long end or by AI sentiment, and at beta 0.94 it remains the lowest-beta name I own. I bought it back below its 200-day and I am not going to be whipsawed out of a 15x compounder at a local low on a macro headline. Stop stays wide at -18%, near $11.73, above the 52-week low; take-profit at +30% lands near $18.59, just inside consensus and the $18.98 high.

Cut three points because the specific claim I made for this position has been tested and partly failed. I sized it as the diversifier that is orthogonal to the AI capex cycle driving CRDO and DDOG, and that remains true — but the shock that actually arrived was a rates shock, and XBI fell 3.48%, the single worst day in my book, because 156 equal-weighted small-cap biotechs are the most duration-sensitive equities in the market. Against a Fed that may hike, this line correlates with the very positions it was bought to offset, so the diversification premium I paid for is not being delivered and the weight comes down to what the standalone case supports. That standalone case is still good and is why I keep 12% rather than exiting: M&A activity and improving regulatory sentiment are genuine drivers, beta is 0.83, and the fund is up 80.7% over twelve months. But it also sits at $162.38 against a $169.89 high, so it is the most extended thing I own going into a hawkish repricing, and buying more of an 80% one-year gain at these levels would convert a hedge into a momentum bet. Stop held at -12%, near $143 — tighter than the book average because biotech gives back fast and this line has the least valuation support of anything I hold, and tightening further would only guarantee a whipsaw in a sector that routinely moves 3% a day.

Cut from 15% to 9% because this is the reassessment at which I said I would size into the print, and a stated plan I decline to execute is worse than no plan. Fiscal Q1 reports Tuesday 1 September, consensus $470.7m and $1.16 against company guidance of $465-475m. The structural case is unchanged and still the best growth-adjusted value I own: 37.5x forward against FY27 guidance of over 80% revenue growth with optical alone above $600m, revenue that tripled to $1.34bn, net income up 805%, 19 analysts at $283.23 with TD Cowen and Barclays at $300. What has changed is that I can now see the shape of the risk more clearly, and it is worse than I assumed. The FY27 guide is explicitly back-half-loaded — mid-single-digit sequential growth in the first half, then acceleration on optical — which means the number that matters Tuesday is not the beat but whether the second-half ramp is reaffirmed without qualification, and back-loaded guides are punished hardest when they are merely maintained. The positioning has also thinned: the stock closed $282.82 on 17 August after an 8.8% run into the event and is now near $233, an 18% de-rate in nine sessions, with hedge fund holders down from 69 to 59 and their dollar value off 24%. At beta 3.23 into a binary event in a tape that just repriced the Fed, a 15% weight risks roughly 3% of NAV on a single session and a bad reaction could plausibly be worse than 20%. Nine percent still expresses a real bet — I want to own the beat — while cutting the single-session damage to something I can survive and redeploy from. Stop stays at -25%, the widest in the book, and take-profit at +35% near $315, both deliberately unchanged: a tight stop through an earnings gap does not protect me, it just converts the gap into a realised loss at the worst tick.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.
novelty: I run only a Round-3 book this experiment, so the cross-round overlap constraint does not bind; what is new here versus the prior construction is that the book stops being six roughly equal expressions of one long-duration growth factor and becomes five positions deliberately spread across three separate drivers — AI-native software demand (DDOG, CRDO), rate and crypto-linked fintech earnings power (HOOD, NU), and M&A-driven biotech (XBI) — with the purest duration bet removed entirely and a third of the book held in cash that now pays more if the thesis risk materialises.
research_notes:
MACRO — the one fact that reorganises the book. On 28 Aug at Jackson Hole, Fed Chair Warsh said 2% inflation is "firm and fixed," that inflation has not meaningfully slowed, and that financial conditions are "not currently restrictive." September fed funds futures repriced from ~35% to 55.7-58% odds of a 25bp HIKE; the 10-year went to 4.73%. Friday: S&P -0.2% to 7,711.76, Nasdaq -0.5% to 26,402.42, Russell 2000 -1.4% to 2,972.37 — small caps took double the large-cap hit, which is the correct read since they carry more floating-rate debt. My entire book keys off one of two factors (AI capex, or the discount rate), and the discount-rate factor just got materially worse: for six weeks I have written that "the long end is at its highs" is what compresses my multiples. It is no longer a level, it is a policy direction.

POSITION MARKS through 28 Aug close vs my 24 Aug entries: DDOG $236.98 (-2.45% Fri, ~flat on week), NET $299.84 (-2.72% Fri, +2.3% on week), CRDO ~$233 (+1% on week), XBI $162.38 (-3.48% Fri, -2.0%), HOOD $104.26 (-5.01% Fri, -3.8%), NU $14.30 (-3.90% Fri, -1.9%). No stops fired. NAV $1,054.15, +5.42%, gross 88%, max DD -10.29%.

CRDO — the event I pre-committed to. Confirmed: fiscal Q1 FY27 reports Tuesday 1 September, 2pm PT. Consensus $470.7m revenue / $1.16 EPS against company guidance of $465-475m (108-113% growth). The guide shape is the risk: management framed FY27 as mid-single-digit sequential growth in H1 then a second-half acceleration on optical (>$600m, with ZeroFlap, silicon photonics PICs and optical DSPs each >$100m). Back-half-loaded guides get punished when the reaffirmation is anything less than emphatic. The stock closed $282.82 on 17 Aug after an 8.8% pre-positioning surge and is now ~$233 — an 18% de-rate into the print — and hedge fund holders fell from 69 to 59 with dollar value down 24%. Beta 3.23.

DDOG — new fact: reports that Palo Alto's $28bn acquisition came after talks with Datadog and Okta fell apart. A named strategic acquirer at the table is a valuation datapoint I did not have. 46 analysts at $285.18 = 20.3% headroom, 89.5x forward, 36% growth, and the OpenAI usage scare is already in the price via the 18% post-earnings drawdown. CEO Pomel sold 47,054 shares at $235.49.

NET — both inputs moved against me. Price rose to $299.84 so headroom fell from 13.8% to 11.2%, while the discount rate that must fall for the thesis to work is now more likely to rise. 202.98x forward, GAAP net loss $102m, and it has filed to sell $2.175bn of convertible senior notes — the associated hedging is real supply. Business is fine (Q2 $696m, +36%, guide raised $58m, FedRAMP High, Kitesurf, Citi $400 / Scotiabank $390).

HOOD — closed $104.26, -5.01% Friday, but every engine improved on the week. BTC ran from ~$72k to $80,258 on 27 Aug (first time above $80k since May) on $1.92bn of spot-ETF inflows, the best week since Oct 2025, before sliding below $78k Friday with the broader risk-off; a $6.4bn Deribit expiry cleared. Interest revenue is up 278% y/y and a hike adds directly to the ~third of revenue that is net interest. Prediction markets and the MIAXdx JV are drawing fresh street targets ($95-115 range; 28 analysts average $120.08). Clarity Act procedural vote due in September — still not law.

NU — $14.30, 14.76x forward, 22 analysts at $18.78 (+31%). Q2: revenue $2.47bn +52%, net income $1.06bn +67%, 33% ROE. New since last week: a $1.0bn buyback authorisation and Mexican banking authorisations, plus an R$45bn Brazil deployment plan. Risk is that higher US rates pressure EM currencies and flows.

XBI — $162.38, 52-week range now $89.33-$169.89, +80.7% over twelve months, 156 equal-weighted names. I bought it as a diversifier against AI-capex risk and it is — but it fell 3.48% Friday, the worst day in my book, on a rates shock. Small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is; its orthogonality is to the risk I hedged, not to the risk that arrived.
